subject: TrueCap #11 — reading an inspection report (don't skim the boring parts)
preheader: The 6 lines that tell you whether to walk · How to price what you find · 3 inspection-stage deals

marketSnapshot.headline: Late-summer market slowing as expected
marketSnapshot.body: Asking rents flat MoM across our covered markets — the seasonal late-summer plateau that hits every August. Days-on-market crept up to 47 from 43 last week, also seasonal. Nothing alarming, just the regular August lull before the September pickup. If you're shopping deals in August, you have meaningfully more negotiating leverage than you'd have in May or October — sellers who've been on-market all summer are getting impatient and will entertain reasonable offers below ask.

dealSpotter.body: Inspector flagged: knob-and-tube wiring in attic (~$4,500 to remediate), roof at end-of-life (~$8,000), and minor foundation settling (cosmetic, $1,500 monitoring + minor fix). Most buyers walk. The smart move: come back with $228k offer citing the inspection report. Seller has been on market 65 days — high probability they accept. The deal at $228k all-in with the work scoped is an 8.6% cap; at $245k with the same work it's only 7.2%. Same property, different deal, depending on how you negotiate.

$152k. Inspector found radon at 6.2 pCi/L (EPA action level is 4.0). Mitigation cost: $1,200-1,500. This is one of those 'sounds scary, costs little' findings — easy to negotiate into the contract. Seller usually pays for radon mitigation when it's flagged at inspection. If they refuse, you absorb the $1,200 and still have a great deal.

$118k 3/2. Looked great on paper. Inspector found settlement crack with vertical displacement >1" — structural engineer review pegged the repair at $12-22k including drainage work. The seller refused to absorb any of it. On a $118k house, that's 10-19% of purchase price. Not the kind of work an absentee landlord should take on for a first or second property. The headline cap rate evaporated in the inspection.

blogFeature.title: Property management yes or no — the actual math
blogFeature.excerpt: PM fees + lease-up + maintenance markup add up to 13-18% of gross rent, not the 8-10% the headline number suggests. When self-management beats PM and vice-versa.

qa.question: I got my inspection report — 40 pages, half of them photos. What do I actually need to focus on?
qa.answer: Six lines decide whether to proceed. Skim past everything else on a first pass. (1) Roof — age, condition, life remaining. A roof needing replacement in the next 2-3 years is $8-15k that needs to be in your offer math. (2) Electrical — panel age and amp service, presence of knob-and-tube or aluminum branch wiring. Knob-and-tube remediation is a $4-12k surprise. (3) Plumbing — main sewer line condition (camera scope is worth it, $300), galvanized vs copper supply lines, water heater age. A failed sewer line is $5-15k. (4) Foundation — any 'structural concerns' note triggers a follow-up structural engineer call. Don't proceed without that second opinion. (5) HVAC — age and condition of furnace and AC. A 20-year-old system is end-of-life. (6) Mold / moisture — any active moisture in basements or attics signals systemic issues, not point-fixes. Everything else (paint chipping, minor caulk gaps, GFCI outlets needing upgrade) is small money. Your offer-revision negotiation should focus on the six above.
